item.title: Association Between Behavioral Activation System, White Matter Microstructure, and Depressive Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Reduced behavioral activation system (BAS) sensitivity is a core behavioral phenotype of anhedonia, a key symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) that involves multifaceted dysfunctions in the reward processing system. However, the white matter microstructural basis of this phenotype remains unclear. We examined fractional anisotropy (FA) in 54 MDD patients and 72 healthy controls (HC) and explored relationships among FA, BAS Total scores, and depressive symptom severity (Beck Depression Inventory, BDI) in MDD patients. All participants underwent diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and completed the BDI, BAS, and Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS) scales. Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to extract FA values from seven a priori white matter tracts. Compared with HC, the MDD group showed significantly lower FA values in six tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, genu of corpus callosum, sagittal stratum, and fornix), as well as significantly lower BAS Total scores and higher BDI scores. Partial correlation analyses within the MDD group showed that FA values in four tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum) were significantly positively correlated with BAS Total scores. Mediation analyses controlling for age, sex, and BIS score revealed that BAS Total scores significantly mediated the relationship between FA values in these four tracts and BDI scores, with an indirect-only mediation pattern. When BIS was tested as an alternative mediator, none of the indirect effects were significant, supporting the specificity of the BAS-mediated pathway. These findings provide new imaging evidence for a "white matter microstructure–behavior–symptom" pathway, suggesting that targeting white matter microstructure and BAS function may help alleviate anhedonia in MDD.

item.title: Brain Structural Changes in Blast-Exposed Special Operations Forces Soldiers.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Special Operations Forces (SOF) soldiers experience frequent low-level occupational blast exposure and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), but the cumulative effects of these exposures on long-term neurological health remain poorly understood. The purpose of this longitudinal cohort study was to investigate associations between occupational blast exposure and brain structural change in SOF soldiers and to determine whether mTBI sustained between assessments moderated these associations. Male SOF soldiers (n = 88) underwent T1- and T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging at two timepoints. Volumetric segmentation was performed using FreeSurfer. Main outcomes were percent change in global brain tissue volumes, including cerebral cortex, cerebral white matter, lateral ventricles, subcortical gray matter, and cerebellar cortex. Exposure was quantified as months between Time 1 and Time 2, used as a proxy for cumulative occupational blast exposure during time in a high-tempo operational unit. The number of self-reported mTBIs sustained between timepoints was categorized as 0, 1-2, or 3 or more injuries. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate. Greater occupational blast exposure predicted increased lateral ventricle percent change (F 1,86 = 9.86; B = 0.126%; R 2 = 0.103; p = 0.002; p -adjusted = 0.012) and decreased cerebellar cortex percent change (F 1,86 = 5.72; B = -0.074%; R 2 = 0.062; p = 0.019; p -adjusted = 0.047). Between-visit mTBI did not significantly moderate these associations. In this cohort of SOF soldiers, greater cumulative occupational blast exposure was associated with lateral ventricular expansion and cerebellar cortex volume loss. The rate of ventricular expansion observed in this study is atypical compared with expected change in healthy adults and may represent an early structural marker of blast-related brain vulnerability. Cerebellar cortex volume loss may reflect regional susceptibility to blast-related injury. Identifying brain structural changes associated with occupational blast exposure may help inform exposure-monitoring strategies and targeted interventions to preserve warfighter brain health and readiness.

item.title: Multivariate Searchlight Decoding of Structural Disconnection and Network Features for Predicting Post-Stroke Deficits.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection analyses have advanced our understanding of post-stroke deficits but remain predominantly based on forward inference, limiting identification of regions specifically predictive of behavioral impairment. We developed a multivariate voxelwise searchlight decoding framework for inverse inference integrating probabilistic structural disconnection with network-topological features. Approach. The analysis included 326 stroke patients from the GRECogVASC cohort assessed six months after stroke. For each patient, an age-specific probabilistic structural disconnection map was reconstructed using normative diffusion MRI tractography from 403 healthy controls. Within each voxel-centered searchlight, four features were extracted: disconnection probability, degree, clustering coefficient, and closeness centrality. Support vector machine classifiers were trained within deficit-specific decoding spaces using balanced bootstrap aggregation and majority voting to predict motor, executive, and processing-action-speed impairments. Statistical significance was assessed using 1,000 permutations, retaining voxels that consistently performed above chance across bootstrap iterations. Decoding-derived regions were subsequently assessed for within-cohort individual-level classification. Main results. Initial validation focused on left and right motor impairments, identifying predictive regions primarily within the contralateral precentral gyrus, internal capsule, and corticospinal tract, with mean accuracy ranges of 68.7-77.9%, 66.4-74.6%, and 64.8-71.8%, respectively. At the individual level, decoding-derived masks preserved overall classification performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 2.6% for individual deficits while reducing voxel dimensionality by up to 95.4%. Executive dysfunction and processing-action-speed deficits showed statistically above-chance but lower accuracies (54.5-66.9%). Executive dysfunction involved predominantly left-lateralized frontotemporal regions, whereas processing-action-speed deficits involved distributed fronto-insular, temporal, parietal, visual-association, and commissural pathways. Significance. The multivariate searchlight decoding framework integrating structural disconnection and network topology provides an inverse-inference approach complementary to lesion- and disconnection-symptom mapping for identifying spatially specific predictive patterns after stroke. The strong motor findings provide proof-of-concept support for the approach, whereas the cognitive results support its extension to distributed behavioral domains while underscoring the need for independent replication before neuroanatomical or clinical interpretation (Clinical trial registration: NCT01339195).

item.title: The anatomo-functional organization of the indirect pallido-subthalamic pathway in humans combining histology and diffusion imaging.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The subthalamic nucleus (STN) integrates cortical motor and emotional information with a posterior motor domain and an anterior limbic domain. However, the detailed anatomo-functional organisation of the STN in humans remains incomplete, largely because the indirect pathway linking the STN and the external globus pallidus (GPe) is difficult to image. Here, we characterize the GPe-STN pathway using histology combined with high-resolution diffusion imaging. We scanned three ex vivo specimens at 11.7 Tesla and ten healthy volunteers at 3 Tesla with ultra-high gradient. Brain sections were immunostained, reconstructed in 3D, and registered to define regions of interest in both datasets. Structural connectivity was assessed using probabilistic tractography (MRtrix), with homogeneously distributed seed points to maximize streamlines reconstruction. We found that GPe-STN streamlines follow fiber bundles that traverse or bypass the internal GP and the internal capsule, ex and in vivo. Ex vivo tractography revealed distinct projection patterns of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor GPe streamlines, targeting the anteromedial STN (24% volume coverage) and the posterocentral STN (67% and 30% coverage, respectively). In vivo tractography revealed a similar spatial organization, particularly in the right hemisphere, with consistent patterns across individuals. A substantial overlap was observed between associative and sensorimotor territories, whereas the limbic territory appeared more segregated. The data-driven clustering of the STN based on GPe-connectivity fingerprints confirms these findings. These results challenge the classical tripartite model of the basal ganglia and provide new insights into the STN anatomo-functional organization and support individualized targeting for functional neurosurgery.

item.title: Ultra-processed food intake during pregnancy and its association with early brain and behavioral development in children: a prospective cohort study.
item.description:
Reviews in endocrine & metabolic disorders
Growing evidence suggests that maternal consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) during pregnancy may adversely affect offspring neurodevelopment. However, the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study combines a comprehensive review of the current literature on maternal UPF consumption during pregnancy, brain development, and behavioral outcomes with empirical evidence from a prospective birth cohort. Specifically, we examined whether neonatal white matter (WM) microstructure may represent a pathway linking maternal UPF consumption with early behavioral development. Data were analyzed from three subsamples of mother-child pairs participating in the Barcelona Life Study Cohort (BiSC; 2018-2021): 560 pairs with maternal dietary and 18-month behavioral data, 43 with maternal dietary and neonatal WM tractography data, and 32 with complete dietary, neuroimaging, and behavioral assessments. Maternal UPF consumption was assessed during the second trimester using food-frequency questionnaires. Neonatal WM microstructure was examined at one month of age using diffusion tensor imaging and deterministic tractography. Behavioral outcomes at 18 months were assessed using the Child Behavior Checklist for Ages 1½-5 (CBCL 1½-5) and the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised (M-CHAT-R). Associations among UPF exposure, WM measures, and behavioral outcomes were analyzed using regression models with permutation testing and hierarchical regression analyses to assess potential mediation. Higher maternal UPFs consumption, was associated with greater behavioural dysregulation at 18 months, including oppositional-defiant, attention, withdrawn, aggressive, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related problems. Maternal UPF consumption was associated with variations in WM microstructure in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum bundle and forceps minor. These variations were further associated with less favorable behavioral outcomes. Diffusivity measures in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus attenuated the association between maternal UPF consumption and oppositional-defiant problems. Findings from both the literature review and cohort analyses support an association between maternal UPF consumption and early behavioral outcomes. Neonatal WM microstructure may represent a potential neurobiological pathway linking maternal dietary habits and early behavioral development.

item.title: MRI Assessment of Baseline White Matter Microstructure and Its Relationship With the Onset and Trajectory of Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment in Breast Cancer Patients.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background White matter microstructure may be affected by cancer and its treatment, yet its association with subsequent cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) remains unclear. Purpose To investigate whether baseline white matter diffusion metrics are associated with the time to CRCI onset and longitudinal cognitive trajectories. Study type Prospective longitudinal study. Population A total of 230 female patients (49.4 ± 8.6 years) with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer (50 Stage II, 180 Stage III) with planned neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery. Field strength/sequence A 3 T, multi-shell SE-EPI DWI. Assessment Diffusion MRI was performed before chemotherapy (baseline). Neuropsychological assessments were carried out at baseline, after the first cycle of chemotherapy, after completion of chemotherapy but before surgery, and at 2-4 years after surgery. Diffusion tensor metrics (mean, radial, and axial diffusivity [MD, RD, and AD]), diffusion kurtosis metrics (axial and radial kurtosis [AK and RK]), and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging metrics (orientation dispersion index [ODI], neurite density index [NDI]) were extracted from 25 white matter tracts, capturing both mean values and peak width. Statistical tests Cox regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed associations with time to CRCI onset and cognitive trajectories, respectively. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant. Results Higher ODI (anterior limb of the internal capsule [ALIC]: HR = 1.28), lower AD (ALIC: HR = 0.72, external capsule [EC]: HR = 0.73, superior fronto-occipital fasciculus [SFO]: HR = 0.70), and greater peak width of AK (ALIC: HR = 1.29, EC: HR = 1.24, genu of the corpus callosum [GCC]: HR = 1.32) were associated with earlier CRCI onset. Lower FA, RK, and MK (β = 0.13 to 0.27 × 10-3 ), higher MD, RD, ODI, and ISOVF (β = -0.23 to -0.13 × 10-3 ), and higher peak width metrics (β = -0.34 to -0.13 × 10-3 ) were associated with poorer longitudinal cognitive trajectories. Conclusions Pretreatment white matter microstructure may help identify patients at greater risk of CRCI and poorer cognitive trajectories. Level of evidence: 2 Technical efficacy Stage 3.

item.title: Whole-Brain MRSI Metabolic Connectomics Reveals Network Disruptions and Altered Gradient Coherence in Psychosis Risk
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain network alterations preceding first-episode psychosis often escape connectomic approaches based on conventional neuroimaging, such as diffusion or functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whole-brain magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) offers a potentially more sensitive alternative: by mapping neurometabolites across the brain, it enables the construction of metabolic connectomes that may capture very early and subtle disruptions of brain network properties. We combined whole-brain proton MRSI, diffusion MRI, and resting-state functional MRI in a sample of 29 individuals meeting DSM-5 criteria for Attenuated Psychosis Syndrome (APS) or Schizotypal Personality Disorder (SCZT), pooled into a single High Risk for Psychosis (HR) group, and 30 healthy controls (HC) to construct metabolic, structural, and functional connectomes. Network-based statistics identified a significant metabolic connectivity subnetwork with higher connectivity in HR than in HC, whereas no corresponding structural or functional connectivity differences were detected. Nodes of this subnetwork had modestly higher structural strength but were not consistently enriched among structural hubs, and no significant regional abnormalities in individual metabolite concentrations were detected. Eigenmode analysis of metabolic connectivity revealed a low-dimensional organization spanning a posterior unimodal-to-transmodal axis and a transmodal-to-limbic axis. Path analysis revealed higher bilateral energy in HR, indicating reduced coherence along a metabolic gradient that parallels the neurodevelopmental sensorimotor-to-association axis. These findings identify whole-brain metabolic network organization derived from MRSI as a systems-level phenotype of psychosis risk and raise the possibility that it captures altered development of large-scale cortical organization.

item.title: Computational model of developmental self-assembly of a cortical microcircuit
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cortical microcircuits emerge from local developmental interactions, yet large-scale computational models typically prescribe connectivity rather than explain its formation. Here we use BioDynaMo to simulate the self-assembly of ~70,000 cortical neurons from 1,200 progenitors in 3D physical space through migration, neurite growth and contact-based synapse formation. With one calibrated filling fraction per connection type, the locally formed synapses reproduce experimentally measured connectivity across 64 connection types (mean absolute error 0.0062) without prescribing individual connections. The grown spiking networks sustain stable, inhibition-dominated activity, and the same developmental rules, given different targets, generate both a canonical cortical microcircuit and a visual-cortex variant. Inverting the migration programme produces a reeler-like column whose aberrant connectivity destabilises network activity. Together, these findings provide a mechanistic link between local developmental processes and the emergence of cortical anatomy, connectivity and function.

item.title: Patterns of Childhood Exposomes, White Matter Development and Behaviors Link to Future Cognition and Psychopathology in Youth
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Environmental exposures during childhood strongly impact individuals' cognitive and socioemotional development, and psychiatric vulnerability. However, childhood exposures rarely occur in isolation. Instead, they form a highly correlated 'exposome' whose multidimensional relationships with brain development and behavioral outcomes remain poorly understood. Elucidating the complex interplay between brain, behavior, and environment requires a multivariate approach. This study used regularized multiset canonical correlation analysis on longitudinal data from 8,113 preadolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study to characterize latent multivariate dimensions linking diverse environmental exposures, tract-wisely resolved measures of white matter (WM) development and integrity, and multi-domain behavioral phenotypes and relate them to concurrent and future psychopathology. Two distinct multivariate dimensions were identified exhibiting different exposure, WM development, and behavior patterns. The first linked greater socioeconomic resources to more advanced WM development, particularly in dorsal-association tracts, and superior cognitive performance. The second dimension linked stronger psychosocial support with higher WM integrity, more advanced development of limbic tracts, and lower levels of psychopathology. Longitudinal analyses revealed differential contributions of these dimensions to follow-up cognitive, socioemotional and psychiatric outcomes. Moreover, WM and exposomic variates in these dimensions moderated the effects of childhood adversity on transdiagnostic psychiatric disorder risk, in sex- and context-specific fashions. Together, these findings clarify how childhood environmental exposures and the linked WM developmental differences relate to cognition and psychopathology risk, potentially informing the identification of candidate neural targets for future interventions.

item.title: Cortical brain changes from early to mid-adolescence in offspring at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: Schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP) emerge in late adolescence or adulthood. Offspring at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ) or BP (FHR-BP) are more likely to develop psychiatric disorders. Prior work from the Danish High Risk and Resilience (VIA) Study found sex-specific volumetric brain differences in offspring at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP aged 11-12 years. This study builds upon these findings by testing whether they reflect group differences in rate of change or stable group differences from early to mid-adolescence. Methods: This study investigated MRI data from offspring at FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population- based controls (PBC) at baseline (11-12 years; n=288) and follow-up (15-16 years; n=249). FreeSurfer longitudinal processing derived total brain volume, cortical measures, and intracranial volume (ICV). Linear mixed-effects models tested group-by-age interactions and sex-specific group effects, as well as associations with psychotic experiences (PE) and lifetime Axis-I mental disorders. Results: The analysis did not detect group-by-age interactions, indicating similar developmental slopes across groups. However, at both time points, males at FHR-SZ demonstrated reduced brain and cortical volumes compared to PBC and FHR-BP males. These effects were attenuated after adjusting for ICV, which was reduced in males at FHR-SZ. The analysis additionally detected volumetric reductions in males with PE, after controlling for risk status. Conclusions: These results extend the previous findings to ages 15-16 years, indicating group differences are stable and persist into mid-adolescence. Associations with ICV suggest early neurodevelopmental effects, and volumetric reductions in males with PE suggest convergent effects with FHR-SZ.

item.title: Expression of the neurodevelopmental disease susceptibility genes CADM1 and CADM2 in the early human fetal forebrain.
item.description:
Journal of anatomy
CADM1 and CADM2 are cell-adhesion molecules with likely roles in cell migration, axon guidance and synapse formation. Both are considered potential susceptibility genes for various neurodevelopmental disorders. However, their expression patterns in early human brain development have not been explored. Here we employed transcriptomics, RNAScope in situ hybridisation (ISH) and immunofluorescence (IF) to determine the time course and location of expression in the human cerebral cortex and thalamus between 7.5-17 postconceptional weeks (PCW). In the cerebral cortex, tissue RNAseq revealed both to be highly expressed throughout this period. CADM1 exhibited very high expression which declined slightly with age. CADM2 exhibited high expression which increased over time. Single-cell RNA-seq and ISH revealed that both genes were co-expressed in most cells; however, IF revealed different patterns of cellular localisation. At 8 PCW, expression for both CADMs was similar throughout the cortex and predominantly located in the cytoplasm/cell surface in the cortical plate (CP) but with stronger expression of CADM1 in the subventricular zone. However, from 10 PCW onwards, the strongest immunoreactivity for CADM1 was in the cell nucleus with weak cytoplasmic localisation, whereas CADM2 was expressed on the cell surface and increasingly in axons with age. By 17 PCW, CADM2 exhibited strong immunoreactivity in the thalamocortical and callosal corticocortical axons but was weakly expressed in corticofugal pathways. In the thalamus, CADM2 expression in posterior and lateral projection neurons contributing to thalamocortical pathways was confirmed. CADM1 and CADM2 show differential expression in the thalamus and associated nuclei, suggesting a role in their segregation; CADM1 favouring anterior and medial thalamic nuclei and the ventromedial subthalamus, CADM2 the lateral habenula, lateral and posterior thalamus and dorsolateral subthalamus. CADM1 and CADM2 may play important and varied roles in early fetal human forebrain development, guiding cell migration and aggregation, and axon guidance and fasciculation.

item.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and language development: biological evidence from an integrative review.
item.description:
Developmental neurorehabilitation
Objective This study aimed to analyze scientific evidence on the relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and its potential implications for language development and speech fluency. Methods An integrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases between August 2025 and July 2026. The search strategy included terms related to vitamin B12, myelination, brain development, language, and speech. Original studies published in English investigating the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency on the central nervous system, neurodevelopment, or structural brain changes were included. Results Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were synthesized through thematic narrative analysis. The findings indicated a relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and delayed neuropsychomotor development, impaired myelination, reduced white matter integrity, and structural brain abnormalities identified by neuroimaging. Furthermore, studies investigating the neural circuits underlying language showed that these same structures are essential for language organization and speech fluency, providing biological plausibility for a potential relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and impairments in these processes. Conclusion Vitamin B12 deficiency may adversely affect neurodevelopment and cerebral myelination, representing a potential mechanism underlying alterations in the maturation of neural circuits involved in language. These findings support the biological plausibility that vitamin B12 deficiency may contribute to impaired language development through disrupted cerebral myelination, although direct clinical evidence remains lacking.

item.title: Olfactory deficits and structural anomalies of the peripheral olfactory system in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Background Approximately 25% of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) develop a psychotic disorder, and the syndrome shares key neurodevelopmental features with psychosis in the general population. The olfactory system develops early in utero, providing a window into gestational disruptions relevant to psychosis risk. We hypothesized that 22q11DS would show impairments in olfactory function and structural anomalies of the olfactory system relative to psychosis spectrum (PS) youth without a known genetic syndrome and typically developing controls (TD). Methods Participants included individuals with 22q11DS (n = 101), PS (n = 56), and TD (n = 52). Sinonasal symptoms, odor identification, and discrimination (Sniffin' Sticks) behaviorally. Structural 3 T MRI measured olfactory bulb volume, sulcus depth, and sulcus length. Sample sizes vary per analysis. Results Relative to TD, 22q11DS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p < .001), lower odor identification (p < .001), and lower odor discrimination (p < .001). PS showed elevated sinonasal burden (p < .001) and marginally lower odor identification (p = .06), but no discrimination deficit. Olfactory bulb volume was significantly smaller in 22q11DS versus TD (p = .007, r = 0.39); PS showed a non-significant trend (p = .07). Olfactory sulcus depth (p = .52) and length (p = .82) did not differ across groups. Conclusions 22q11DS is associated with elevated sinonasal burden, robust olfactory identification and discrimination deficits exceeding those of PS and reduced olfactory bulb volume. The co-occurrence of functional deficits and reduced bulb volume without sulcal anomalies may distinguish the 22q11DS olfactory phenotype from that of PS. These hypothesis-generating findings are consistent with partially dissociable neurodevelopmental mechanisms and support the utility of 22q11DS as a genetic model for psychosis risk.

item.title: Neurochemical signatures of morphometric network reorganization in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Links to cognition and behavior.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Objective Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is associated with neurocognitive behavior problems and regional morphometric abnormalities, yet large-scale brain network reorganization and its molecular correlations remain unclear. Here, we explored whether remodeling of the individual-level morphological similarity network (MSN) in DMD aligns with specific neurotransmitter systems and associates with cognitive, behavioral, and motor performance. Methods We studied 111 boys with DMD and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Individual MSNs were derived from T1-weighted MRI. Global and nodal graph-theoretical metrics were compared between groups, and network-based statistics (NBS) were used to identify altered subnetworks. Spatial correlations linked altered MSN maps to normative PET/SPECT neurotransmitter maps, and Spearman correlations related MSN alterations and neurochemical indices to clinical measures. Results The global small-world organization of MSNs was preserved. However, boys with DMD showed increased degree centrality (DC) in the bilateral hippocampus and left cerebellar lobule 3, and decreased DC in the right cerebellar lobule 7b. NBS identified a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit characterized by reduced morphological similarity. MSN alterations showed significant spatial associations with dopaminergic, serotonergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, cholinergic, and endocannabinoid systems, and the strength of these associations and network disruption were associated with poorer cognitive, motor, and behavioral performance. Conclusions Children with DMD exhibit MSN remodeling centered on a cerebellar-frontotemporal-subcortical morphological circuit that is neurochemically coupled to specific neurotransmitter systems and linked to cognitive, behavioral, and motor deficits. This study elucidates potential neurochemical mechanisms underlying neurobehavioral abnormalities in DMD and may provide biological insights to inform the development of neuromodulation-based therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Cortical morphometric similarity alterations and molecular correlates in acute ischemic stroke.
item.description:
Neuroradiology
Purpose Ischemic stroke is associated with distributed cortical structural alterations, but the molecular context of acute-stage morphometric similarity (MS) changes remains unclear. This study aimed to characterize MS alterations in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and examine their spatial transcriptomic correlates using the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Methods In this cross-sectional case-control study, 36 patients with first-ever AIS involving the unilateral basal ganglia and/or corona radiata and 36 healthy controls (HCs) were included. Patients were enrolled within 7 days after symptom onset, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in the acute stage. Whole-brain MS networks were derived from multiple cortical morphometric features. Group differences in regional MS were assessed with adjustment for age, sex, education, and infarction volume. Spatial associations between MS alterations and gene expression were examined using partial least squares regression with post-mortem transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Correlations between regional MS values and plasma metal concentrations were examined in patients with AIS. Results AIS patients exhibited regionally heterogeneous MS alterations, with increased MS mainly in the lateral occipital, lingual, postcentral, and pericalcarine cortices, and decreased MS mainly in the superior frontal, precuneus, and superior temporal regions. Imaging-transcriptomic integration showed that these spatial MS changes were associated with gene expression profiles related to neuronal viability, transcriptional co-regulation, and cellular stress-related pathways. After permutation testing and false discovery rate (FDR) correction, significant associations were identified between right precuneus MS and plasma lead (Pb) and cesium (Cs) levels. Conclusions These findings identify region-specific MS alterations in AIS and provide spatial transcriptomic context for early post-stroke structural changes.

item.title: Structural changes in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex following a randomized clinical trial of virtual reality-based cognitive remediation in mood and schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Introduction Cognitive impairments are common in patients with mood disorders (MD) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) and impair quality of life. Developing pro-cognitive treatments is hindered by limited understanding of the biology underlying cognitive impairment and improvement. This structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study examined the neural correlates of cognitive improvement following a Virtual-Reality-based Cognitive Remediation Therapy (VR-CRT) intervention. Methods Patients underwent eight VR-CRT or VR-control treatment sessions during a four-week period. The study population included data from a transdiagnostic subsample of 41 symptomatically stable, cognitively impaired patients with MD or SSD (VR-CRT: n = 22; VR-control: n = 19) with baseline structural MRI data of which 33 (VR-CRT: 20; VR-control: n = 13) also underwent MRI at treatment completion. Neuropsychological assessment was completed both pre- and post-treatment and additionally at three-month post-treatment follow-up. Results Gray matter volume in the VR-CRT group increased over time in the right caudal middle frontal gyrus (MFG) compared to VR-control. Secondary hypothesis-driven analysis showed a similar increase in right caudal MFG thickness for VR-CRT patients. These structural changes were not associated with treatment-related cognitive improvement. However, greater left rostral MFG thickness at baseline was associated with more cognitive improvement over time in the VR-CRT group. Conclusion This study demonstrates treatment-related structural changes in the right caudal MFG and suggests that baseline left rostral MFG thickness may represent a candidate marker of cognitive improvement within the VR-CRT group. These findings support further investigation of MFG structure as a marker of brain response and cognitive treatment outcome. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06038955, and is completed.

item.title: Differential structural profiles of the hippocampus and thalamus and their cognitive relevance in unilateral mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Background Cognitive dysfunction is common in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), yet how much the hippocampus and the thalamus each contribute remains unclear. We compared fine-grained hippocampal and thalamic structure and their cognitive relevance in unilateral MTLE. Methods We studied 71 patients with unilateral MTLE (39 with hippocampal sclerosis [HS], 32 without) and 17 controls. FreeSurfer-derived cortical, hippocampal-subfield, and thalamic-nucleus volumes were compared using permutation-based general linear models. In patients, 19 cognitive measures were related to volume using covariate-adjusted partial correlations under seizure-referenced (ipsilateral/contralateral) and anatomical left/right codings. Nested additive models tested the incremental cognitive contributions of hippocampal and thalamic volume. Results Relative to controls, patients showed widespread thalamic atrophy (34 of 44 nuclei in the full cohort, 32 of 44 in each subgroup), whereas hippocampal subfield atrophy was largely confined to HS and no cortical region survived correction. All 48 corrected volume-cognition associations involved hippocampal subfields; none involved thalamic nuclei. Additive models showed that ipsilateral hippocampal volume explained 7.4%-14.6% of cognitive variance alone and explained an additional 6.8%-18.9% of cognitive variance beyond thalamic volume, whereas global thalamic volume did not add significant corrected incremental variance. Preserving anatomical hemisphere linked verbal comprehension and naming to left hippocampal subfields and working memory predominantly to right subfields. Conclusions Hippocampal and thalamic abnormalities showed distinct structural and cognitive profiles in unilateral MTLE. Thalamic atrophy was widespread, whereas hippocampal volume was more closely related to cognition and showed additional variation by HS status and anatomical hemisphere.

item.title: Regional cortical thinning in cerebral small vessel disease: associations with disease burden and cognitive and motor impairment.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a major cause of cognitive decline and mobility impairment, yet whether cortical thickness and cortical volume provide similar or complementary information across different levels of CSVD burden remains unclear. We examined regional cortical thickness and cortical volume in healthy controls and participants with CSVD using high-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging and FreeSurfer-based parcellation. Greater CSVD burden was associated with thinning across bilateral insular, occipital, temporal, cingulate, and cuneal regions, whereas cortical volume alterations were more spatially restricted, with only the left parahippocampal gyrus surviving Bonferroni correction. After adjustment for demographic characteristics, vascular risk factors, apolipoprotein E genotype, and mean cortical thickness, associations remained evident in the bilateral insulae and selected occipital and temporal regions. Regional cortical thickness was also related to cognitive and mobility performance. Exploratory incremental analyses showed that regional cortical thickness remained associated with cognitive performance in several regions after accounting for the corresponding regional cortical volume, intracranial volume, and other covariates. These findings suggest that cortical thickness and cortical volume may capture partly distinct aspects of cortical morphology in CSVD, with cortical thickness potentially providing complementary information related to cognitive performance.

item.title: Early and premature menopause and brain health across the adult lifespan: a scoping review of neuroimaging and neuropathological outcomes.
item.description:
Maturitas
Early-onset menopause may have detrimental impacts on brain health, yet mechanisms underlying this association are poorly understood. This scoping review synthesizes findings linking early and premature menopause to brain health across adulthood, including brain volume, function, and pathology. We conducted a scoping review using Covidence literature review software with a comprehensive search strategy using search terms related to early and premature menopause and brain health. The authors independently mapped study details onto a data-extraction tool to ensure inter-rater agreement. We reviewed 21 studies sorted into two categories by primary exposure: 1) early age at menopause (n = 10), and 2) premenopausal bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (PBSO) (n = 11). Nine of the 10 papers that focused on early age at menopause reported at least one association with poorer brain outcomes, including smaller volumes and greater pathology. Brain regions reported to be associated with earlier menopause in multiple studies included the medial temporal lobe (i.e., hippocampus and parahippocampus). Multiple studies observed associations with lower total gray matter volume and poorer white matter integrity. Among papers that focused on PBSO, 7 reported worse brain outcomes and 4 originating from the same parent study reported results that were not easily characterized in terms of our hypothesis (i.e., group differences were attributable to the interactions of estrogen use, age, or other factors with PBSO). Despite inconsistency in definitions, methodologies, and populations of interest, over three-quarters of papers we reviewed reported poorer brain health associated with premature and early menopause. Studies did not consistently evaluate or interpret these associations in terms of potential confounders or mechanistic explanations. Future research would benefit from studies designed to evaluate underlying neural mechanisms and increased measurement accuracy for menopause type and timing.

item.title: Brain structural features of treatment resistant depression in a large Italian sample: A multimodal imaging study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Major depressive disorder is a common psychiatric condition characterized by persistent low mood, emotional dysregulation, and cognitive impairments affecting daily functioning. Approximately 30% of patients fail to respond adequately to at least two antidepressant trials, a condition known as treatment resistant depression (TRD), the neurobiology of which is still poorly understood. This study therefore aimed to investigate grey matter (GM) and white matter (WM) alterations associated with treatment resistance, directly comparing patients with TRD, treatment-sensitive depression (TSD), and healthy controls (HCs). MRI data were acquired from 294 individuals with MDD (193 TRD and 101 TSD) and 72 HCs. Group differences were assessed using analyses of variance followed by post-hoc t-tests. Compared with TSD patients, TRD patients showed reduced GM volume in striatal, temporal, and medial orbitofrontal regions. Relative to HCs, TSD patients exhibited localized GM reductions in the anterior cingulate cortex, whereas TRD patients showed extensive reductions across frontal, temporal, parietal, and limbic areas. Significant differences also emerged in WM microstructural integrity, as measured by fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MD). Compared with both TSD patients and HCs, TRD patients exhibited widespread FA reductions paralleled by increased AD, RD, and MD values, whereas no significant differences emerged between TSD patients and HCs. These findings provide evidence that TRD is characterized by a distinct neurobiological profile, offering new insights into the mechanisms of treatment resistance that may ultimately facilitate the development of more effective, tailored therapeutic interventions.

item.title: Behavioral dimensions and white matter organization in early childhood following preterm birth
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype. While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization. Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk. Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro- and macro-structure in young children born preterm. Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks). Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning. Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors. Results: In the preterm sample, autism- and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension. In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum. No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or full-term samples. Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.
