item.title: Cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss: linking brain structure, glymphatic function, and molecular mechanisms.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
The neurobiological mechanisms of cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) remain unclear. This study examined multi-level neural mechanisms from macroscale gray matter (GM) structure, microscale glymphatic function, and imaging transcriptomics. Sixty-nine ARHL patients and 76 controls underwent multimodal MRI and neuropsychological assessments. Glymphatic function was assessed via DTI-ALPS index and choroid plexus volume (CPV). Transcriptomic analysis using Allen Human Brain Atlas identified molecular pathways and key genes linked to GM atrophy. ARHL patients showed GM atrophy in right amygdala, left inferior frontal gyrus, and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but increased volume in left cerebellum. They also exhibited reduced ALPS index and enlarged CPV. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of glymphatic function on visual memory via right amygdala volume. Transcriptomics revealed enrichment in axonogenesis, energy metabolism, and protein ubiquitination, with key drivers including SMURF1 and GAD1. ARHL-related cognitive decline may follow a cascade from sensory deprivation to glymphatic dysfunction, involving energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, and axonal remodeling, ultimately leading to degenerative atrophy and compensatory adaptation in specific brain networks.

item.title: Examining the Relationship Between Regional Vulnerability and Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescents: The Potential Mediating Role of Cognition.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are subclinical hallucinations or unusual thought content that, when distressing or persistent, signal heightened risk for psychosis spectrum disorders and cognitive impairments. We used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study (N = ∼11,800) to examine if structural brain deviations toward neuropsychiatric disorders, quantified using disorder-specific Regional Vulnerability Indices (RVIs), were associated with distressing PLEs at age 13-14, and whether cognition mediated these relationships. Cortical and subcortical RVIs were calculated for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, metabolic disorder, and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that higher cortical RVIs for schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease, bipolar disorder, metabolic disorder, and Parkinson's disease-and all subcortical RVIs-were significantly associated with greater distressing PLE severity. Both cortical and subcortical RVIs were negatively associated with fluid and crystallized cognition, with subcortical RVIs showing the largest effects. Mediation analyses indicated that crystallized cognition, and to a lesser extent fluid cognition, mediated many RVI-distressing PLE relationships. These findings suggest that neuroanatomical differences confer risk for psychotic-like experiences partly through their impact on cognitive development. The results highlight RVIs as sensitive markers of distributed brain vulnerability in youth and suggest that cognitive function, particularly crystallized ability, is a potential pathway linking brain structural alterations to emerging psychotic symptoms.

item.title: Information, Mass, Energy Principles: A biophysical and ecological framework for understanding the brain.
item.description:
Bio Systems
The brain is a highly complex biological system whose structure, function, and evolution are constrained by material resources and energy availability, as any other natural system. Here, we extend the ecological Information-Mass-Energy (IME) framework (Peñuelas, 2024) to neuroscience. In contrast to purely computational models, we propose that the brain is an information-organizing system constrained by mass availability, energetic expenditure, and thermodynamic efficiency. Through comparative analyses across mammalian species, we identify a superlinear scaling relationship between white and grey matter volumes, alongside a positive association between white matter volume and inhibitory-control performance. This suggests that neural organization contribute to cognitive capacities beyond brain size alone. Integrating these findings with metabolic scaling principles, we propose that brain evolution involves trade-offs between increasing informational complexity and the material and energetic costs required to sustain it. Within this framework, we formulate testable hypotheses concerning how informational organization may scale with neural material and energetic expenditure. Furthermore, we introduce a quantitative disturbance-recovery model that incorporates carrying capacity, recovery rate, and disturbance magnitude and duration, generating testable predictions for neurological conditions such as stroke and neurodegeneration. By combining empirical scaling relationships with a mathematical framework for neural organization, energetic constraints, and resilience, the IME framework offers a novel biophysical and ecological perspective on brain evolution and function. This framework also provides a foundation for investigating energetically sustainable information processing in biological and artificial systems.

item.title: Can qualia be geometric? A geometro-diffusion framework for the relational structure of color experience.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
Within the Geometro-Diffusion Theory (GDT) of consciousness, we formulate a candidate geometry for the relational organization of color experience. We distinguish a diffusion-induced scaffold, the color content encoded on it, and its neuronal realization. Elementary network examples establish these distinctions and show how consensus-directed nonlinear activity preserves the diffusion scaffold. On a 76-region human structural connectome, a distributed encoding is learned from 16 controlled colors and then frozen. Evaluation on 256 new colors gives a Spearman correspondence of 0.919 with the CIEDE2000 perceptual reference, compared with 0.923 for direct CIELAB distances. Nonlinear Izhikevich encoding followed by the same anatomical propagation gives analytic-neuronal correspondence of 0.924. The learned construction therefore transfers color relations to new stimuli and expresses much of their geometric organization through nonlinear neuronal activity. Connections with predictive coding and cortical gradients identify possible roles for the geometry of anticipated and stimulus-evoked responses. Within GDT, intrinsic access and recursive use link this relational organization to qualitative experience. The results provide a mathematical and computational candidate for that organization, together with explicit empirical comparisons for evaluating its experiential interpretation. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10577-2.

item.title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

item.title: Location matters: The link between regional white matter hyperintensity burden and subjective cognitive decline in those at risk of Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundSubjective cognitive decline (SCD) is a potential early indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). While SCD has been linked to white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden, it is unclear whether regional WMH lesion volume is differentially associated with domains of cognitive complaints.ObjectiveExamine whether regional WMH burden is associated with domain-specific SCD (memory, executive function) in cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of AD.MethodsParticipants were 150 cognitively unimpaired older adults (65-89 years) with subjective memory complaints and a first-degree family history of AD. Cognitive complaints were assessed with the Cognitive Change Index (CCI-20). WMHs were quantified from T1-weighted and FLAIR MRI using an automated pipeline and categorized into sample-based tertiles for total, subcortical, and lobar regions. Hierarchical regressions examined associations between WMH burden and CCI-20 memory, executive, and total scores, while adjusting for demographics, total intracranial volume, MRI site, APOE ε4 status, and mood symptoms.ResultsGreater WMH burden in the left temporal lobe was associated with increased memory complaints and total SCD, whereas no WMH region was associated with executive function complaints. APOE ε4 status and depressive symptoms were associated with greater memory and total cognitive complaints across models. Apathy was uniquely related to memory complaints.ConclusionsAmong older adults with elevated risk of AD, memory-SCD was associated with greater region-specific left temporal cerebrovascular lesion volume. Findings highlight the clinical relevance of left temporal WMH burden and the importance of considering regional vascular pathology, genetic risk, and mood when characterizing early subjective cognitive changes.

item.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

item.title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
item.description:
The Journal of head trauma rehabilitation
Objective To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. Setting Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. Participants Canadian Armed Forces breachers (n = 30) and snipers (n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls (n = 57). Design MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. Main measures High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. Results Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. Conclusion Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

item.title: Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Post-stroke depressive symptoms are common, but studies on the contributions of lesion locations to depression symptoms remain inconsistent. Bayesian statistics offer the possibility to clarify these inconsistencies by providing evidence in favor and against observed associations. We reanalyzed four previously published observational cohorts with 1,864 patients with stroke characterized for depressive symptoms from France, Korea, Germany and the USA. We performed voxel-wise Bayes factor mapping using general linear models. Lesion maps were used to test for associations of post-stroke depressive symptoms with lesion location. Network level associations were tested based on structural disconnection and functional lesion network maps estimated by reference to normative connectome data. Due to a sample size with broad lesion coverage, Bayesian inference was informative in large parts of the brain. Lesion associations were found in clusters in the right hemisphere including cortical (frontal, insular, parietal) and subcortical regions (striatum, amygdala, hippocampus) and adjacent white matter. Evidence of no contribution to post-stroke depressive symptoms was observed in large parts of the left hemisphere. Structural disconnection was linked to depressive symptoms in the bilateral frontal white matter prominently involving the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation. Lesion network mapping revealed evidence of an association of post-stroke depressive symptoms with network connectivity in the left posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and less consistently, the bilateral anterior insula, along with widespread absence of associations in other regions. Depressive symptoms were most strongly associated with right frontal lesions and right-dominant structural disconnection in frontal cortico-subcortical circuits.

item.title: Changes in brain structural connectivity networks are associated with electroconvulsive therapy efficacy in adolescents with major depressive disorder and suicidal ideation.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Suicide is a leading cause of death among adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD). Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) effectively alleviates depressive symptoms, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. 27 adolescents with MDD and SI and 32 demographically matched healthy controls were included. This study used structural magnetic resonance imaging and graph theory analyses to examine group differences in the global and nodal network topology at baseline and longitudinal changes within the MDD group following ECT. Linear mixed-effects models, correlation analysis, and machine learning were employed to further investigate the relationship between network topological properties and clinical symptoms. At baseline, adolescents with MDD exhibited reduced global normalized clustering and decreased nodal centrality across networks, with abnormalities predominantly in the limbic and sensorimotor systems. Following ECT, group differences in global network metrics were no longer significant, and topological abnormalities in networks related to emotional regulation and cognitive control were ameliorated. However, persistent topological disruptions in the sensorimotor and visual networks remained. Compare to topological metrics, machine learning models leveraging raw structural connectivity matrices demonstrated superior predictive performance for clinical efficacy. This study offers novel insights into the disorder's neurobiological mechanisms and the therapeutic effects of ECT.

item.title: Interhemispheric structural connectivity alterations and hierarchical connectome gradient reorganization following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Neurological sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection extend beyond the acute phase, yet the structural basis of network-level brain changes across disease severity remains poorly understood. We investigated structural brain connectivity and connectome gradient organization in adults with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), stratified into non-hospitalized and hospitalized groups, alongside a comparison group with non-COVID respiratory infection, using 3T diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging. Network-Based Statistics was used to identify subnetworks of altered structural connectivity, and connectome gradients were derived separately for each hemisphere using diffusion map embedding and compared across groups within seven canonical resting-state networks. Network-Based Statistics identified a predominantly interhemispheric subnetwork differing across the three groups, linking left-hemispheric control and salience regions to right hemisphere sensory and association areas, with a related subnetwork distinguishing hospitalized participants from the comparison group. Connectome gradient analysis revealed group-related differences in connectivity-derived embedding positions within sensorimotor and dorsal attention networks, more pronounced among hospitalized participants. These findings suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with severity-related interhemispheric structural connectivity differences and altered hierarchical connectome organization, particularly within sensorimotor and dorsal attentional systems. Given the cross-sectional design, modest sample size, and absence of behavioral data, these findings should be considered exploratory and do not establish anatomical fiber loss, causal mechanisms, or predictive clinical value; instead, they provide a structural framework to guide future studies of neurological outcomes after COVID-19.

item.title: Associations among interleukin-6, superior frontal gyrus thickness, and executive control in long-term high-altitude migrants.
item.description:
Acta psychologica
This study examined how systemic inflammation, prefrontal cortical structure, and executive control performance are related in long-term high-altitude residents. A total of 129 healthy Han Chinese adults who had relocated from low-altitude regions and were living and working in Lhasa, Xizang (3650 m) underwent hematological testing, structural MRI, and an Attention Network Test (ANT). Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) concentration was obtained from clinical blood reports, cortical thickness of the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) was extracted using FreeSurfer, and executive control efficiency was indexed by the conflict effect in the ANT (lower scores indicating better performance). Partial correlations and mediation analyses (PROCESS Model 4) were conducted, controlling for age, gender, and hypoxic exposure duration. IL-6 concentration was significantly negatively correlated with executive control scores (r = -0.22, p = 0.04), indicating that higher IL-6 levels were associated with better executive control efficiency, whereas no significant associations were found with alerting or orienting. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of IL-6 on executive control via left SFG thickness (indirect effect = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.003]), with a significant total effect (-0.218, 95% CI [-0.429, -0.007]) and a nonsignificant direct effect (-0.194, 95% CI [-0.403, 0.014]). These findings suggest that relatively higher IL-6 concentrations within the physiological reference range are associated with better executive control performance, with left SFG cortical thickness showing a significant statistical indirect association. Together, these results highlight a potential immune-structure-cognition relationship in long-term high-altitude migrants, although comparative and longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these associations are specifically related to high-altitude exposure.

item.title: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader–Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

item.title: Early WM Alterations after Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: An Exploratory Study Using Quantitative MRI and DTI.
item.description:
AJNR. American journal of neuroradiology
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The purpose was to investigate early WM alterations in patients with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) within 1 week of trauma using quantitative MRI and DTI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 31 patients with mTBI and 36 healthy controls. Neuropsychological assessment and MRI scans were performed within 1 week of trauma. ROIs were selected from 4 WM regions: superior longitudinal fasciculus, anterior limb of the internal capsule, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Quantitative MRI and DTI were used to assess WM alterations. Correlation analyses explored relationships between WM alterations and clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Compared with controls, patients with mTBI demonstrated lower scores on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, particularly in the domains of abstraction, delayed recall memory, and orientation. Higher T1 values were detected in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule, whereas elevated proton density (PD) values were found in the right external capsule, bilateral superior longitudinal fasciculus, and posterior limb of the internal capsule. No significant differences in T2 or fractional anisotropy were observed. PD values in the left posterior limb of the internal capsule were negatively correlated with attention and language scores in patients with mTBI. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, quantitative MRI may detect subtle WM alterations in the acute stage of mTBI. No notable between-group differences were observed in the DTI parameters in the current cohort. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine the reproducibility, temporal evolution, and clinical relevance of these findings.

item.title: Multimodal MRI reveals brain structural and functional abnormalities associated with wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Objectives The pathogenesis of the wearing-off (WO) phenomenon in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains unclear. This study aims to explore the abnormalities in brain structure and function among PD patients with WO. Methods A total of 39 PD patients with wearing-off (PD-WO) and 43 PD patients without wearing-off (PD-nWO) were prospectively enrolled. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was employed in this study to evaluate structural differences, and functional connectivity (FC) was used to assess functional differences between the two groups. Results Compared with PD-nWO patients, PD-WO patients showed significantly reduced gray matter volume (GMV) within the left middle occipital gyrus (MOG.L), bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG.L/R), as well as the left triangular division of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFGtriang.L). Regarding functional connectivity, PD-WO patients exhibited widespread abnormalities, including weakened connectivity in the cerebellar-basal ganglia-sensorimotor cortex circuits, hippocampus-postcentral gyrus, and cerebellar-occipital (cuneal cortex) pathways, as well as enhanced connectivity between cerebellar subregions and between the cerebellum and occipital cortex (lingual gyrus) and parahippocampal gyrus. Conclusions This preliminary single-center cross-sectional study revealed significant differences in brain structure and function between PD-WO and PD-nWO patients. These findings provide a better understanding of the neural mechanisms behind the WO phenomenon in PD and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

item.title: Quantitative anatomy of the human striatum suggests limited synaptic plasticity and higher structural stability in the intermediate putamen than in the nucleus accumbens.
item.description:
Neuroscience
The striatum is the input nucleus of the basal ganglia and receives convergent projections from the cerebral cortex, the thalamus, the amygdala, and the substantia nigra. The topographical organization of these synaptic projections provides the connective bases for the functional subdivision of the striatum into sensorimotor, associative, and limbic domains, that are largely homogeneous in cellular composition due to the predominance of medium spiny neurons. In spite of this homogeneity, there are several molecular, cellular, and biochemical differences that could contribute to the connection-based functional specialization and to differences in disease vulnerability between striatal sectors. In the present article we analyze postmortem striatal tissue from neurotypical human donors to identify cellular and molecular factors that could underlie functional specialization and selective vulnerability across the human striatum. We quantify neuronal morphological features related to genetic expression and protein synthesis, molecular markers that promote either synaptic plasticity or structural stability, and gene expression data in two striatal regions: the limbic nucleus accumbens and the sensorimotor intermediate putamen. Our analyses reveal larger neuron bodies, higher expression of markers that inhibit synaptic plasticity in the intermediate putamen and higher expression of markers thar promote synaptic plasticity in the nucleus accumbens. These findings support the notion that the intermediate putamen is characterized by enhanced structural stability and limited plastic potential, in contrast to the greater adaptability preserved in the nucleus accumbens.

item.title: Degree-biased diffusion geometry of networks. Implications for network neurosciences.
item.description:
Mathematical biosciences
Degree-biased diffusion gives unequal directional influence to the two ends of an undirected edge. Its propagator is therefore nonsymmetric, and it generates two geometries. The column geometry compares the responses to perturbations at different sources, and the row geometry compares the observations across the same family of perturbations. We show that both geometries are Euclidean at finite times, but they can differ in their transient behavior and in their long-time limits. In contrast with standard diffusion, individual distances can expand temporarily even while the dynamics approach consensus. Degree-biased diffusion conserves a degree-weighted quantity instead of the ordinary network mass. An exact transport-and-reservoir decomposition identifies the local exchange responsible for this difference. Degree-biased Laplacians also arise exactly as the linearization of the dynamic mean-field model of large-scale brain activity when the long-range synaptic coupling is modulated by inverse receiver and sender gains. This gives them a neurobiological interpretation and a physical time scale. On a 76-region human structural connectome, degree bias changes the pairwise proximity, the geometrically optimal routes, and the regions visited by those routes. Hubs-attracting diffusion produces an earlier and higher maximum of column signature information than standard diffusion, while it reduces the row maximum. Hubs-repelling diffusion increases both maxima, but it reaches them later. The number of source responses needed to reconstruct the row kernel also depends strongly on the sampling order. In particular, high-degree sources are favored under attraction and low-degree sources under repulsion. These results characterize how a fixed network can generate distinct relational geometries under different propagation laws. Here, we treat geometric routes as distinct from literal signal trajectories, and mathematical reconstruction as distinct from evidence of conscious access.

item.title: A reproducible pipeline for simulating individual and inter-brain neural dynamics from structural connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of neuroscience methods
BACKGROUND: Computational models can link anatomical structure to neural dynamics. However, there is no validated, reproducible pipeline that simulates individual and inter-brain EEG-like dynamics from an individual's own structural connectome. NEW METHOD: To address this, we developed a comprehensive computational pipeline that combines probabilistic tractography from Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) with dynamical systems modeling to simulate EEG-like neural dynamics from individual connectomes. It extracts anatomical connectivity, intra-individual functional connectivity, and inter-individual (two-brain) functional coupling features. It then evaluates their group-discriminative information with random-forest classification under repeated nested cross-validation. Simulated phase-locking values are calibrated against empirical resting-state EEG. RESULTS: In a test sample of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and matched controls (16 each), simulated intra-individual synchrony added classification information beyond anatomy, raising accuracy from 71.2% (AUC 0.843) to 77.6% (AUC 0.871), in a sample where groups did not differ in mean structural connectivity. COMPARISON WITH EXISTING METHODS: Unlike current single-brain simulations, this pipeline generates and jointly simulates two individual brain models within a single system, and reports the contribution of each feature level explicitly. CONCLUSIONS: The pipeline provides a reproducible, extensible framework for deriving informative individual-level dynamic features from anatomy. The two-brain extension generates and ranks candidate inter-brain features, providing a principled way to identify between-brain measures for hypothesis-driven testing.

item.title: Posterior fossa syndrome.
item.description:
Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
Posterior fossa syndrome (PFS), also known as cerebellar mutism syndrome (CMS), is a distressing postoperative complication affecting children undergoing craniotomy for infratentorial tumors, most frequently medulloblastoma. It is characterized by a distinct latency period followed by mutism, profound emotional dysregulation, and a broad spectrum of cerebellar motor and cognitive deficits. Diffusion MRI and tractography have consistently shown that structural damage to the proximal efferent cerebellar pathway-specifically the dentato-rubro-thalamo-cortical tract within the superior cerebellar peduncle-is strongly implicated as the anatomical driver of PFS. Historical series favored the telovelar over the transvermian surgical approach, although recent prospective multicenter data demonstrate equivalent risks between the two techniques, shifting the neurosurgical focus toward meticulous surgical technique and minimizing damage to eloquent tissue around the fourth ventricle. Validated clinical scoring tools, such as the Posterior Fossa Syndrome Questionnaire, standardize clinical phenotyping and are making their way into clinical practice. Increasingly advanced risk prediction models allow for precise preoperative risk stratification based on objective imaging markers. Pharmacological interventions, including zolpidem and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, have shown limited efficacy in mitigating acute symptoms. Although near-universal clinical improvement occurs over time, long-term neurocognitive and motor sequelae remain highly disabling. Combining advanced neuroimaging, sophisticated risk modeling and meticulous microsurgical technique offers the best paradigm to shift the narrative of PFS from an expected complication to a preventable one.

item.title: Regional Mitochondrial Density Maps Selective Posterior Atrophy in Parkinson's Disease.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
BACKGROUND: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathobiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the spatial relationship between regional energetic demand and patterns of neurodegeneration remains poorly understood, limiting mechanistic insight and development of disease-modifying therapies. OBJECTIVES: This study tested whether regional mitochondrial density aligns with patterns of brain atrophy in PD, how this alignment differs across genetic groups, and whether the mitochondrial-atrophy axis associates with motor and cognitive features. METHODS: Structural magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 849 individuals (210 healthy controls, 639 patients with PD). Principal component analysis (PCA) identified dominant atrophy axes and tested their association with regional mitochondrial density and complex I activity. Transcriptomic validation used Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression data restricted to 924 MitoCarta-annotated genes across 31 cortical regions. RESULTS: Participants with PD exhibited higher volumetric loss in limbic and subcortical regions than controls. PCA showed a posterior cortical axis of atrophy (PC3) that correlated positively with regional mitochondrial density and was more strongly expressed in LRRK2-PD than in sporadic PD. This axis was selectively associated with visuospatial dysfunction. Transcriptomic validation confirmed that regions of greater atrophy preferentially expressed mitochondrial genes, with mitoribosome assembly, mitochondrial DNA maintenance, and coenzyme Q biosynthesis emerging as the strongest pathway-level predictors. CONCLUSION: These findings link the brain's regional mitochondrial landscape to spatially patterned neurodegeneration in PD, with amplification in LRRK2 mutation carriers. This mitochondrial atrophy axis may provide a biologically informed marker aiding patient stratification and mitochondrial-targeted therapeutic development. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children’s memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score . Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults’ movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult’s propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child’s brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children’s memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns. Significance Statement Despite decades of research establishing potential mechanisms of infantile amnesia, little is known about the maturation of neural memory representations across development, limiting progress in developmental memory research and educational applications. This study reveals a developmental trajectory of memory: children show adult-like processing in the IT area by age 3, the hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions by age 7, reflecting mature perceptual, memory, and multimodal and social-affective processing, respectively. The left posterior hippocampus is crucial for the maturation of adult-like memory patterns. These findings show that (i) ResMem DNN can help educators select dynamic stimuli that are memorable to children by age 4, and (ii) our cross-validated model enables assessment of memory maturation without explicit memory measures.

item.title: White-matter microstructural alterations and cross-sectional thyroid hormone-cognition associations in hypothyroidism.
item.description:
European thyroid journal
PURPOSE: Hypothyroidism is associated with cognitive and emotional dysfunction, which may be accompanied by alterations in white-matter (WM) microstructure. However, few studies have compared diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures and clinical correlates across overt hypothyroidism (OH), subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH), and healthy controls (HCs). We investigated DTI-derived WM microstructural measures and their associations with thyroid function and neuropsychiatric performance in adult-onset hypothyroidism. METHODS: We enrolled 44 patients with OH, 41 with SCH, and 53 HCs. Thyroid function, neuropsychiatric assessments, and DTI data were collected. Age, sex, and years of education were entered simultaneously as covariates in all inferential group-comparison models, exploratory two-sided partial Spearman correlations, and exploratory cross-sectional indirect-effect models, except when these covariates themselves were the descriptive variables compared. RESULTS: Both OH and SCH groups had lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores and higher depression scores than HCs. Compared with SCH and HCs, the OH group showed more extensive between-group differences in DTI-derived metrics; no SCH-HC differences survived family-wise error correction. Within the OH group, DTI measures showed nominal, covariate-adjusted exploratory associations with thyroid hormone concentrations and neuropsychiatric scores. Exploratory covariate-adjusted models identified indirect associations of total triiodothyronine (TT3) and total thyroxine (TT4) with MoCA through fractional anisotropy (FA) of the left posterior thalamic radiation (PTR). The corresponding total and direct associations were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, OH was associated with more extensive differences in DTI-derived WM measures than SCH. The exploratory indirect associations through left PTR FA do not establish a temporal or causal pathway.

item.title: Healthy Sleep Mitigates the Association Between Cardiometabolic Disease and Poorer Cognitive and Brain Health.
item.description:
Journal of the American Heart Association
BACKGROUND: Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and stroke, are important risk factors for dementia. We examined whether healthy sleep can support cognitive and brain health in people with CMDs. METHODS: The study included data from 408 977 adults from the UK Biobank. CMDs were defined using medical records, medication use, and medical history. Sleep patterns were defined using a composite score incorporating sleep duration, chronotype, insomnia symptoms, snoring, and daytime sleepiness. A subsample (n=34 913) underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging; volumes of total brain, gray matter, white matter, hippocampus, and white matter hyperintensities were ascertained. Associations of joint CMD (yes/no) and sleep (healthy, intermediate, poor) status with global and domain-specific cognitive scores and brain magnetic resonance imaging measures were examined using linear regression models. RESULTS: At baseline, 54017 (13.2%) participants had at least one CMD. In joint exposure analysis, performance in global cognition (β=0.02 [95% CI, 0.01-0.05]), verbal/numeric reasoning (β=0.07 [95% CI, 0.01-0.12]), and processing speed (β=0.07 [95% CI, 0.04-0.10]) was significantly higher among individuals with CMDs and a healthy sleep pattern, compared with those with CMDs and a poor sleep pattern. Similarly, in neuroimaging analyses, participants with CMDs and a healthy versus poor sleep pattern showed significantly larger total brain volume (β=0.22 [95% CI, 0.08-0.35]), gray matter volume (β=0.23 [95% CI, 0.09-0.36]), and white matter volume (β=0.19 [95% CI, 0.05-0.33]). CONCLUSIONS: Healthy sleep may attenuate the associations of CMDs with poorer cognitive performance and markers of brain atrophy. The findings highlight sleep as a modifiable factor that may support cognitive and brain health in individuals with CMDs.
